problems.memo_sentence: The paper targets pricing European-style options by solving the Black–Scholes partial differential equation (PDE), framed as determining the present option value under the Black–Scholes model with terminal payoff boundary conditions.
problems.source_evidence: "the Black-Scholes model, a linear parabolic partial differential equation with terminal value given by the pay-off of the option contract and no additional boundary conditions."
problems.explanation: The memo states terminal payoff boundary conditions but omits the paper's explicit statement that there are no additional boundary conditions. That caveat is part of the problem framing in the source.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors map the Black–Scholes PDE, after a log-price change of variables and time reversal, into a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian (the Black–Scholes Hamiltonian) so that option price dynamics can be treated as a Schrödinger-type evolution suitable for quantum simulation.
problems.source_evidence: "Moreover, we show that this method is also applicable to time-dependent volatility PDEs, for which non closed-form solution exists in general." and later "The natural question that arises now is whether a choice of σ(ˆx) can maintain the sparsity of the Hamiltonian or if the system can be approximated by a controllable sparse Hamiltonian... Further investigation will be dedicated to studying this case in detail in subsequent works."
problems.explanation: The memo presents the method as if it solves the Black–Scholes PDE generally, but the paper explicitly says the time-dependent volatility case is not resolved and is left for future work. That limitation is important to the scope of the contribution.

problems.memo_sentence: The approach is a digital, gate-based Hamiltonian simulation algorithm for the non-Hermitian Black–Scholes Hamiltonian, implemented by embedding its non-unitary propagator into a larger Hilbert space via unitary dilation that uses a single ancillary qubit and post-selection to recover the desired dynamics.
problems.source_evidence: "we embed the time propagator into an enlarged Hilbert space, making use of only one ancillary qubit, using a technique known as unitary dilation."
problems.explanation: The paper describes embedding the time propagator, not specifically the Hamiltonian, into the enlarged Hilbert space. The memo shifts the object of the embedding from the propagator to the Hamiltonian, which is a different claim.

problems.memo_sentence: The method exploits the decomposition of the Hamiltonian into commuting Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts, treats the resulting operator as 1-sparse, and uses quantum signal processing with analytically known eigenvalues to construct the required simulation oracle; measurement relies on post-selection on the ancilla and can be combined with quantum amplitude estimation for more efficient sampling of option price amplitudes.
problems.source_evidence: "Currently, quantum signal processing (QSP) techniques offer the most efficient quantum algorithms for quantum simulation of sparse Hamiltonians, as mentioned in [70]." and "The oracles needed for this QSP methodology provide a description of the Hamiltonian... In this sense, in order to build the oracle that returns the value of the Hamiltonian eigenvalues, which are analytically known, one might use the results in Ref. [102]."
problems.explanation: The paper does not claim to construct a QSP oracle from analytically known eigenvalues as part of its own method; it says one might use a cited method for that oracle. The memo turns this into a direct methodological claim of the paper.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors claim that their QSP-based Hamiltonian simulation provides a feasible route to solving option price dynamics and that, with nine qubits on a fault-tolerant device (eight for spatial discretization plus one ancilla), they can reach accuracy levels comparable to classical numerical algorithms for the Black–Scholes PDE.
problems.source_evidence: "We report expected accuracy levels comparable to classical numerical algorithms by using 9 qubits to simulate its dynamics on a fault-tolerant quantum computer" and later "Our perspective for a future work is to introduce errors associated to NISQ devices in order to analyze the realistic implementation in a near-term quantum platform."
problems.explanation: The memo captures the 9-qubit claim but omits that the paper frames this as an expected accuracy level on a fault-tolerant device and explicitly leaves NISQ/noisy implementation for future work. That is a meaningful limitation on the result's practical scope.
